prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic timekeeping to a fractional uncertainty of about 1e-18

statement.case_for: I opened with IceCube (B043) first, but the opening ballots show B059 is the candidate on which the committee's evidence is most convergent: seven of eight members ranked it, four placed it in their top three, and the two members closest to the physics (Kroll and Lindroth) put it first. As an instrument builder I weigh heavily a case in which a concept (Katori's magic-wavelength lattice trapping) and a demanding experimental realisation (Ye's record accuracy and stability, and the many-body clock work) combine into a measurement tool that changed what can be measured. Fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 have been reproduced by independent laboratories in strontium, ytterbium and other species, the redefinition of the second is under active discussion, and the applications (relativistic geodesy, searches for varying constants and for new physics) are concrete. The two-name configuration is clean and does not force an arbitrary third slot, which is the main failure of B016, B019 and B043 in this list. Maturity is high and attribution is the most defensible among the shortlisted candidates.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is a refinement of a field already honoured: Hall and Haensch (frequency combs, 2005), Wineland (ion control and ion clocks, 2012) and earlier laser-cooling prizes cover neighbouring ground, so the committee must be satisfied that the lattice clock is a distinct and sufficient achievement and not an engineering sequel. Other groups (JILA/NIST, SYRTE, PTB, Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow) also reached world-class accuracy, so a Katori-Ye pairing leaves real credit questions. Finally, redefinition of the second has not happened, so part of the impact is prospective. If the committee prefers a discovery about nature over a measurement advance, B043 or B034 would be the better choice.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B059 first: Katori's magic-wavelength concept and Ye's record clocks make optical frequency metrology the leading precision tool, with a clean two-person credit and independent confirmation, and the comb and ion-clock prizes do not break the pairing.
responses.response: I did not rank B059 in my own top eight, and I now think that was an underweighting of how complete the evidence is. I agree with Kroll on maturity and on the clean pairing. I would qualify one point: his claim that the 2005 and 2012 prizes 'do not break' the pairing rests on the citation being narrow. The citation has to name the lattice clock and its accuracy, not frequency metrology generally, or the overlap objection becomes serious. I also share his unease about weighing Ye against other groups, because the NIST/JILA and European contributions to the 1e-18 milestones cannot be neatly separated from his.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B059 first and stresses the control of lattice-induced shifts, blackbody and many-body systematics, independent confirmation in several laboratories, and that the two-name configuration avoids a contested third slot.
responses.response: Her argument about systematics is the one that persuades me, since a metrology prize stands or falls on whether the claimed uncertainty is real, and independent comparisons settle that. I disagree mildly with the idea that avoiding a third slot is itself a point of merit; it is a convenience, and I would not want B059 to win simply because it is easy to allocate. Her point that Hall-Haensch and Wineland force a judgement about incremental novelty is the open question I carry into the next round, and I would like her to say what the lattice clock added in kind and not only in degree.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B016 first and B034 second, and notes for B034 that the superconducting mechanism and full phase diagram are unresolved, so any citation should be limited to flat bands and correlated states; he also doubts that IceCube source identification is complete.
responses.response: I agree with both reservations, and they are why I moved my preference away from B043 and B034. On IceCube, the diffuse flux is secure but the source picture is incomplete, which I accepted in my opening and now weigh more heavily. On B034, I accept a narrowly worded citation as workable, but his own estimate that recognition is 'a little early but defensible' is a weaker ground than the maturity of B059. I disagree that B016 is clearly ahead of B059: the Hasan versus Mele versus Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang question is a real attribution problem that he acknowledges and does not resolve.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks DMFT (B046) first and B016 second, argues that B034 is probably slightly early compared with candidates whose theory is settled, and questions whether a metrology prize should outrank condensed-matter candidates.
responses.response: I take his maturity argument against B034 seriously and have changed my own placement of it accordingly: I keep it as an alternative rather than my preferred choice. I disagree with the framing that a precision-measurement prize versus a condensed-matter prize is merely a committee-balance question, since it is partly an evidential one: the lattice clock has a quantitative, independently verified result, while the central open question in moire matter is still the mechanism. I note that B046 received only one ranking and that no colleague defended its attribution, so I cannot support it on this record.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B016 first, argues the 2016 prize covered topological phases in general and not this concrete discovery, and says the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio is clean with Hasan and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang left out.
responses.response: Her point that the 2016 prize did not cover the spin Hall state and Z2 insulators specifically is a fair rebuttal to the overlap worry raised by Danielsson and Johansson. Where I differ is on 'clean': a trio that omits both the three-dimensional discovery by Hasan and the HgTe proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is cleaner only if one accepts the exclusion, and I do not think the committee has yet argued that. I would support B016 if the credited-name question can be settled, but on the current record I rate its attribution below that of B059.

uncertainties: Whether the lattice clock is judged a sufficiently distinct achievement given the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
How to weigh Katori and Ye against other lattice-clock groups (NIST/JILA, SYRTE, PTB) whose contributions to the 1e-18 milestones are not credited.
Whether the committee prefers a discovery about nature (B043, B034) over a measurement advance when the evidence on maturity is comparable.

For B043, whether source identification will mature enough, and how to apportion credit among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the AMANDA and Baikal predecessors; I have not independently verified individual roles.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for B059, B034, B016, B013 or B025. I note adjacent experience: my profile documents experimental astroparticle and gamma-ray work (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur) which is close to B043, and a CERN-based PhD in experimental particle physics which is close to B019. No documented tie to IceCube, ATLAS or CMS is recorded, so I do not claim a recusal need, but I will flag it if either becomes a final configuration.
